tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

content.content:
Exit code 1
# Constitution

The rules the process itself is subject to. Specifications, designs, code and agents are
subordinate to this document; where anything below disagrees with it, this document wins.

Every article carries an enforcement level. **[CRITICAL]** blocks a merge, and an agent is to
stop and escalate rather than work around it. **[SHOULD]** is a strong default whose departure
needs a reason recorded in the change. **[MAY]** is guidance.

Changing an article requires an ADR in [`ADR/`](ADR/).

---

## Article I — The specification is the source of truth [CRITICAL]

Behaviour is described in `spec/` before it is built. Code contradicting `spec/` is either a
defect in the code or a change not applied to the specification. It is never an accepted
divergence, and "the code is the documentation" is not an answer this project accepts.

It is the specification, not the code, that the next person reads at three in the morning. The
code says what happens; only the specification says what was *meant* to happen — and that is the
only thing that lets anybody tell a feature from a bug.

## Article II — Requirements are testable sentences with identifiers [CRITICAL]

A requirement uses the EARS keywords — `WHEN`, `WHILE`, `IF … THEN`, `WHERE` — together with
`MUST` or `SHALL`. Never *should*, *may*, *could*, *probably* or *etc.* A requirement that
cannot be failed cannot be satisfied.

Every requirement carries a unique identifier scoped by its change (`CR-2608-a7f3/R-3`) and
every one has acceptance criteria written as Given/When/Then. A criterion no observer could
check is not a criterion.

## Article III — Every requirement is proved by a test [CRITICAL]

No requirement travels without at least one test that refers to it by identifier. The reference
is mechanical — a `req` marker, a Gherkin tag or the identifier in a test's name — and the
`specs` gate checks both directions: a requirement nothing refers to fails, and a reference to a
requirement that does not exist also fails. The second half matters more than the first, because
a typo is what every traceability scheme actually dies of.

Where a requirement genuinely cannot be tested automatically, it says so about itself in its own
text (`**Verified-by:** manual — <reason>`). The exception is then counted and printed, and that
is the difference between a gap considered and a gap passed over.

## Article IV — The specification changes on the same branch as the code [CRITICAL]

A change of behaviour and the specification edit that describes it land in one pull request.
Never in the next one. The next one guarantees a window in which the trunk describes code that
no longer exists, and it rests on a step nobody is blocked by.

Every edit under `spec/` is declared in that change's `delta.md` as `ADDED` / `MODIFIED` /
`REMOVED` together with a `**Why:**`. The declared set and the actual diff must be *equal* — an
edit absent from the delta fails, and a delta entry with no edit also fails.

## Article V — Non-goals are written down [SHOULD]

Every change says what it deliberately does **not** do. Silent scope is what makes a reviewer
and an author finish agreeing about two different things, and what turns a "missing" feature
into an argument six months later rather than a decision anybody remembers.

## Article VI — A rule the database does not hold is not a rule [CRITICAL]

A constraint the application relies on and the storage layer does not enforce is a constraint
that falls over under concurrency. Business uniqueness is a unique index rather than a
convention: a rule checked by read-before-write passes every sequential test and lets two
concurrent requests through. The same principle governs every boundary: the contract is the
authority and the code is validated against it, not the other way round.

## Article VII — Ambiguity is a question, never an improvisation [CRITICAL]

Where a requirement, a field, a label or a rule is unclear, the process stops and asks a human.
It does not pick the more likely reading and does not rationalise the choice in an artefact
where the next reader will take it for a decision.

The question is closed — two to four options, the recommendation first, each with its
consequence in one sentence — with free text always available. A free-text answer is
interpreted, announced and recorded; it never produces the same question a second time.

## Article VIII — A divergence is a measurement and it edits the specification [CRITICAL]

Independent artefacts are produced in parallel from one specification, and a disagreement
between them is not an accident to patch. It is a measurement of where the specification was
ambiguous.

Every settled disagreement is followed by an edit to the *earliest* document which, had it been
clearer, would have prevented it. Fixing only the artefact at the end of the chain leaves the
ambiguity in place, and the next change walks into it again.

A ruling may be taken automatically **only** when it follows f

... [3952 characters truncated] ...

xception extends to that path and to nothing else.

Authentication, personal data and every regulated surface require a human decision. An agent
escalates; it never merges such a change on its own.

## Article XII — The project's scripts are the interface [CRITICAL]

Every task is a script. Run the script, never a command from inside it: each checks its own
prerequisites, and those checks exist because their absence produced failures that took a day to
find. `scripts/check.sh` is the definition of "will CI pass" — a gate added to CI belongs there
too, and a fitness function proves the two lists are equal rather than believing they are.

There are two interfaces, and which directory a script sits in says which one it is.

[`scripts/`](../scripts/) is the **human's** interface to the application — running, testing,
linting, migrating. Run by a person or by CI. Every task exists there as **one** `.sh` script
over the shared `_lib.sh`; task scripts written in Python are libraries that the `.sh` calls,
not a second entry point to the same task.

The scripts are POSIX and that is a decision rather than neglect
([`design/conventions.md`](design/conventions.md) § Scripts). Windows is supported through WSL
or Git Bash and through nothing else; a named absence of support is more honest than a second
copy of every script that diverges in the week nobody is looking at it.

[the engine](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/skills/_shared/sdd/) is the **agent's** interface to
the change *process*. Called by the skills that name it, from the repository root, one
implementation per platform. It ships with those skills — in the plugin, not in this
repository — so that a skill and the script it calls change together, and `skill_lint.py`
breaks the build when they do not. The process's own
commands under [the process's own `bin/`](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/bin/) are the bridge — its CI runs a shell script, and
the shell script runs Python. `scripts/` is the application's interface and never calls the
process; what the process may call in `scripts/` is the script contract
([`script-contract.md`](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/docs/script-contract.md)).

Rejected (decision of 2026-09-09, `cr: historical` — the process became independent of the
application it works on: a template ships `scripts/` and a stack profile, the process ships
the process's own commands and reads the profile; two trees, two CIs, one contract between them): a script
in `scripts/` as the bridge from the application's CI into the process. It made the application
depend on the process, in the one direction the split forbids, and it put a gate the process
owns into a list the template's CI keeps.

Neither directory is a place to opt out of anything. Both are covered by `ruff` and
`mypy --strict`; choosing a folder has never been a way to lower the standard here.

## Article XIII — Allowed and forbidden [CRITICAL]

**Allowed.** Python ≥ 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2.0 with Alembic, Pydantic 2, PostgreSQL 16 and
only it ([`design/architecture.md`](design/architecture.md) § One engine), `uv` in the range
`>=0.12,<0.13`; TypeScript 5.9, React 19, Vite, TanStack Query, react-hook-form with zod,
Tailwind 4 over CSS design tokens; pytest, pytest-bdd, vitest, testcontainers; Playwright
(Chromium alone) only in `e2e/ui/` — [`design/testing.md`](design/testing.md) § The UI smoke in
a browser.

**Forbidden.** Business logic in routers. `fastapi` or `starlette` imported from `services/`,
`models/` or `schemas/`. `create_all()`. A raw hex colour or a magic pixel size in a component.
A file named `utils.py`, `helpers.py`, `common.py`, `format.ts` or `utils.ts`. Star imports,
with one mechanical exception documented in
[`design/architecture.md`](design/architecture.md). Unpinned tool versions in a gate. Logging
secrets, tokens or personal data.

## Where the process's own files are named

Rejected (decision of 2026-09-09, `cr: historical` — the change process left this repository
for the plugin `forge@scalo`. Article XII still holds word for word: a tool the stack
profile refuses is not run by hand, and the process's own commands are the bridge from the
process into Python. What changed is only where those commands come from — they arrive on
PATH with the plugin instead of sitting in a directory of this repository's — so the article's links now name
the repository that ships them. No article was reworded; `spec/ADR/` stays empty until the
first change goes through `/forge:sdd`, and framework changes are made on the trunk and carry no
`delta.md`): rewording Article XII to describe a plugin. The article is about not assembling

# Constitution

The rules the process itself is subject to. Specifications, designs, code and agents are
subordinate to this document; where anything below disagrees with it, this document wins.

Every article carries an enforcement level. **[CRITICAL]** blocks a merge, and an agent is to
stop and escalate rather than work around it. **[SHOULD]** is a strong default whose departure
needs a reason recorded in the change. **[MAY]** is guidance.

Changing an article requires an ADR in [`ADR/`](ADR/).

---

## Article I — The specification is the source of truth [CRITICAL]

Behaviour is described in `spec/` before it is built. Code contradicting `spec/` is either a
defect in the code or a change not applied to the specification. It is never an accepted
divergence, and "the code is the documentation" is not an answer this project accepts.

It is the specification, not the code, that the next person reads at three in the morning. The
code says what happens; only the specification says what was *meant* to happen — and that is the
only thing that lets anybody tell a feature from a bug.

## Article II — Requirements are testable sentences with identifiers [CRITICAL]

A requirement uses the EARS keywords — `WHEN`, `WHILE`, `IF … THEN`, `WHERE` — together with
`MUST` or `SHALL`. Never *should*, *may*, *could*, *probably* or *etc.* A requirement that
cannot be failed cannot be satisfied.

Every requirement carries a unique identifier scoped by its change (`CR-2608-a7f3/R-3`) and
every one has acceptance criteria written as Given/When/Then. A criterion no observer could
check is not a criterion.

## Article III — Every requirement is proved by a test [CRITICAL]

No requirement travels without at least one test that refers to it by identifier. The reference
is mechanical — a `req` marker, a Gherkin tag or the identifier in a test's name — and the
`specs` gate checks both directions: a requirement nothing refers to fails, and a reference to a
requirement that does not exist also fails. The second half matters more than the first, because
a typo is what every traceability scheme actually dies of.

Where a requirement genuinely cannot be tested automatically, it says so about itself in its own
text (`**Verified-by:** manual — <reason>`). The exception is then counted and printed, and that
is the difference between a gap considered and a gap passed over.

## Article IV — The specification changes on the same branch as the code [CRITICAL]

A change of behaviour and the specification edit that describes it land in one pull request.
Never in the next one. The next one guarantees a window in which the trunk describes code that
no longer exists, and it rests on a step nobody is blocked by.

Every edit under `spec/` is declared in that change's `delta.md` as `ADDED` / `MODIFIED` /
`REMOVED` together with a `**Why:**`. The declared set and the actual diff must be *equal* — an
edit absent from the delta fails, and a delta entry with no edit also fails.

## Article V — Non-goals are written down [SHOULD]

Every change says what it deliberately does **not** do. Silent scope is what makes a reviewer
and an author finish agreeing about two different things, and what turns a "missing" feature
into an argument six months later rather than a decision anybody remembers.

## Article VI — A rule the database does not hold is not a rule [CRITICAL]

A constraint the application relies on and the storage layer does not enforce is a constraint
that falls over under concurrency. Business uniqueness is a unique index rather than a
convention: a rule checked by read-before-write passes every sequential test and lets two
concurrent requests through. The same principle governs every boundary: the contract is the
authority and the code is validated against it, not the other way round.

## Article VII — Ambiguity is a question, never an improvisation [CRITICAL]

Where a requirement, a field, a label or a rule is unclear, the process stops and asks a human.
It does not pick the more likely reading and does not rationalise the choice in an artefact
where the next reader will take it for a decision.

The question is closed — two to four options, the recommendation first, each with its
consequence in one sentence — with free text always available. A free-text answer is
interpreted, announced and recorded; it never produces the same question a second time.

## Article VIII — A divergence is a measurement and it edits the specification [CRITICAL]

Independent artefacts are produced in parallel from one specification, and a disagreement
between them is not an accident to patch. It is a measurement of where the specification was
ambiguous.

Every settled disagreement is followed by an edit to the *earliest* document which, had it been
clearer, would have prevented it. Fixing only the artefact at the end of the chain leaves the
ambiguity in place, and the next change walks into it again.

## Article XII — The project's scripts are the interface [CRITICAL]

Every task is a script. Run the script, never a command from inside it: each checks its own
prerequisites, and those checks exist because their absence produced failures that took a day to
find. `scripts/check.sh` is the definition of "will CI pass" — a gate added to CI belongs there
too, and a fitness function proves the two lists are equal rather than believing they are.

There are two interfaces, and which directory a script sits in says which one it is.

[`scripts/`](../scripts/) is the **human's** interface to the application — running, testing,
linting, migrating. Run by a person or by CI. Every task exists there as **one** `.sh` script
over the shared `_lib.sh`; task scripts written in Python are libraries that the `.sh` calls,
not a second entry point to the same task.

The scripts are POSIX and that is a decision rather than neglect
([`design/conventions.md`](design/conventions.md) § Scripts). Windows is supported through WSL
or Git Bash and through nothing else; a named absence of support is more honest than a second
copy of every script that diverges in the week nobody is looking at it.

[the engine](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/skills/_shared/sdd/) is the **agent's** interface to
the change *process*. Called by the skills that name it, from the repository root, one
implementation per platform. It ships with those skills — in the plugin, not in this
repository — so that a skill and the script it calls change together, and `skill_lint.py`
breaks the build when they do not. The process's own
commands under [the process's own `bin/`](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/bin/) are the bridge — its CI runs a shell script, and
the shell script runs Python. `scripts/` is the application's interface and never calls the
process; what the process may call in `scripts/` is the script contract
([`script-contract.md`](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/docs/script-contract.md)).

owns into a list the template's CI keeps.

a browser.

with one mechanical exception documented in

secrets, tokens or personal data.

# When the process is the thing that is broken

*A shared contract. The worker contract quotes it as rule 15, and the injected session context
as iron rule 12, instead of describing it in words of their own.*

---

## The principle

> **Working around the process is a finding ABOUT the process. Where the fault cannot be fixed
> from the tree you are standing in, the finding is a ticket — filed at the moment you have the
> evidence, not at the end of the session that had it.**

The process already knows how to be wrong loudly: a gate goes red, a hook refuses, a skill
returns `FAILED`. What it did not know how to be is wrong *quietly* — a rule bent rather than
broken, a step improvised because none was written, a script run once to get past something.
Every one of those passes every gate, and every one of them is the process telling you
something it has no other way to say.

Which repository can fix it is not a judgement: `sdd-ownership` answers it. Whose fault it is
*is* a judgement, and § 8 of the intake form is where you argue it.

## The signals

### Measured — the session audit already counts these

`session_audit.py` names them from a transcript, hours later. Meeting one *while you are
working* is the same finding, earlier and with the evidence still in hand.

| What it counts | What it means |
|---|---|
| `improvisation -- code written in the command rather than in a file` | a `python3 -c`, a `node -e`, a heredoc fed to an interpreter: code with no file, no test and no second reader |
| `improvisation -- a script written on the fly instead of a verb` | you wrote a `.py` or `.sh` to get past something, and the process has a verb for it or ought to |
| `improvisation -- a program in argv` | a chain of commands long enough to be a program somebody will have to read once and never again |
| `art. XII --` | a tool the stack profile refuses, run directly rather than through the script that wraps it |

And the four hatches, which are **counted rather than forbidden**. Each is a legitimate move
that somebody signed for. A hatch used once is a decision; a hatch used as a road is the
finding, and the second time is when to say so.

| What it counts | The move |
|---|---|
| `escape hatch -- a stage closed on a red gate` | `--accept-red` |
| `escape hatch -- lowering the path below the arithmetic` | `--allow-lower` |
| `escape hatch -- preempting the change slot` | `--force-parallel-hotfix` |
| `escape hatch -- the question queue was skipped` | `ask --now` |

### Judged — no pattern catches these, and they are the ones that cost most

- **You improvised a step.** The stage said what to produce and no skill said how, so you
  decided. That decision was not reviewed by anybody and is now in the artefact.
- **You rationalised a rule into not applying here.** `verification.md` already names the
  shape: *"I will use different words and the rule will not apply."* If the argument for
  skipping something took more than one sentence, that is the signal.
- **You repaired the process to get the task done.** You edited a skill, a gate, a profile or
  a script because it was in your way. Whether or not the edit was right, the task was the
  reason — and a repair whose reason was impatience is a repair nobody reviewed.
- **An instruction named something that is not there.** A skill told you to read a file, run a
  command or cite a document that does not exist on this stack. An instruction that cannot be
  carried out is not a thing to route around; inventing the missing input is how fabricated
  data gets into an artefact.
- **The same failure twice.** The orchestrator already calls this out — *"the same failure
  twice is not an iteration"* — and the second time is the finding, not the third.

## Which document wins

Two live documents used to give opposite orders and nothing ranked them. **This one wins, and
the worker contract with it.** A project's own `CLAUDE.md` — a template's, or an instance's —
describes its tree; it does not get to say who in this process may post outward, because the
half that may is a property of the process and not of the stack. Where a `CLAUDE.md` says *file
it immediately*, it is describing **the orchestrator's half**, which is true, and it is not
addressing a dispatched worker, which cannot.

And the label is **never** a thing a document writes down. `sdd-ownership` computes it from
GitHub's own record of the lineage — `from-template` from a template, `from-instance` from an
instance — so a `--label` written into an instruction is a value that was right once. Fourteen
issues in this register carry `from-template` and were raised from an instance repository; that
is what a typed label looks like a year later, and it is why no verb below takes one.

## What you do

Three steps, in this order. They cost one command and one paragraph.

1. **Bank it, then file it — and do not stop to ask.** Banking is first because it cannot fail:

   ```bash
   sdd-engine change_state add-fault --cr <CR> --signal '<what it did, and what it cost>' \
     --owner engine
   ```

   `--owner` is the judgement and it takes one of three words: `engine`, `template`, or `here`
   for a fault this level owns and repairs rather than files.
   It writes the fault into the change record with the destination and its label **computed**,
   allocates it a `PROC-n`, and refuses nothing for want of a network. A second report of the
   same fault inside one change is the same row with `seen` counted up, not a second ticket.
   Then `fault-report` fills the form and runs one `gh issue create` against the address that
   was computed, and:

   ```bash
   sdd-engine change_state resolve-fault --cr <CR> --id PROC-n --filed <url>
   ```

   Do not search for a duplicate first — a duplicate costs a close and a link, a report lost
   with the session that found it costs the evidence. This is the intake rule that already
   governs a template filing upward, and it governs this for the same reason.

   **`gh` absent, unauthenticated, issues disabled, no network?** That costs the filing and it
   does not cost the finding: `resolve-fault --id PROC-n --unfiled --reason '<which of those>'`
   is a legal ending, the retro reports it, and the work carries on.
2. **Record the workaround where somebody will find it.** § 12 of the form has the field, and
   it asks the question that matters: must this be reverted when the fix lands, and where does
   the revert belong. *A workaround nobody removes becomes the behaviour.*
3. **Go on with the work.** The ticket is the record, not a gate. Cite its URL in the pull
   request body and in the change record or the changelog entry.

## Who files, and who reports

**A dispatched worker never files.** It touches no git, asks no user and posts nothing outward
— rules 2, 7 and 11. What it does is say so in one line of its closing block:

```
- PROCESS_FAULT: NONE | <the signal, and what it cost>
```

The orchestrator reads every report and files from the main conversation, before the stage
closes. **It banks the line in the same write that banks the return**, which is the mechanism
rather than the rule:

```bash
sdd-engine loop back --member <skill> --process-fault <skill>='engine:<the line it reported>'
```

That flag exists because the line used to have one reader and one fate. It reached the
orchestrator's context and nowhere else, so a wave that ended before it was acted on ended the
finding with it — and there was no moment at which anybody could see that a fault had been
reported and never filed. Now the queue is in the record, `loop next` carries the open ones in
its digest every turn, and the only way one leaves is with a URL or with a reason.

`sdd-retro` is the backstop and not the mechanism: it *reads the queue*, records which faults
were filed and names the ones that were not, and it files nothing itself — a skill that finds
and files its own findings is a skill grading its own work. Before the queue it had nothing to
read, so it was discovering for the first time, hours later, that nothing had been filed.

## What this rule does not do

**It is not a licence to skip the step.** A filed ticket says the process was in your way; it
does not say you may go around it. Where a refused preflight, a red gate or a hook's refusal
stands between you and the work, it still stands after you have filed — *"a refused preflight
is not something you work around."*

**It is not for an ordinary failure.** A test that fails, a gate that is red, a requirement
that contradicts another: those have their own routes — the debug ladder, the coherence gate,
`NEEDS_DECISION`. This is for when the *process itself* was the obstacle.

**It is not a counter.** One issue per distinct fault. Filing the same thing four times in one
session is noise, and noise is how a signal stops being read: *a rule with a false alarm
produces a red people silence, and then it stops working where it was right as well.* The
queue takes the cheap half of that off you — two members of one wave reporting the same fault
land on one `PROC-n` with `seen: 2` — and leaves the judgement, which is yours.

**It is not a gate.** Nothing in `close_stage` reads the queue. A fault that could not be filed
because somebody's token expired must not stop the product work that has nothing to do with it;
the digest carries it, the retro reports it, and neither refuses. An unfiled fault is a visible
debt, never a blocked stage.

| `improvisation -- a script written on the fly instead of a verb` | you wrote a `.py` or `.sh` to get past something, and the process has a verb for it or ought to |
| `improvisation -- a program in argv` | a chain of commands long enough to be a program somebody will have to read once and never again |
| `art. XII --` | a tool the stack profile refuses, run directly rather than through the script that wraps it |

And the four hatches, which are **counted rather than forbidden**. Each is a legitimate move
that somebody signed for. A hatch used once is a decision; a hatch used as a road is the
finding, and the second time is when to say so.

| What it counts | The move |
|---|---|
| `escape hatch -- a stage closed on a red gate` | `--accept-red` |
| `escape hatch -- lowering the path below the arithmetic` | `--allow-lower` |
| `escape hatch -- preempting the change slot` | `--force-parallel-hotfix` |
| `escape hatch -- the question queue was skipped` | `ask --now` |

### Judged — no pattern catches these, and they are the ones that cost most

- **You improvised a step.** The stage said what to produce and no skill said how, so you
  decided. That decision was not reviewed by anybody and is now in the artefact.
- **You rationalised a rule into not applying here.** `verification.md` already names the
  shape: *"I will use different words and the rule will not apply."* If the argument for
  skipping something took more than one sentence, that is the signal.
- **You repaired the process to get the task done.** You edited a skill, a gate, a profile or
  a script because it was in your way. Whether or not the edit was right, the task was the
  reason — and a repair whose reason was impatience is a repair nobody reviewed.
- **An instruction named something that is not there.** A skill told you to read a file, run a
  command or cite a document that does not exist on this stack. An instruction that cannot be
  carried out is not a thing to route around; inventing the missing input is how fabricated
  data gets into an artefact.
- **The same failure twice.** The orchestrator already calls this out — *"the same failure
  twice is not an iteration"* — and the second time is the finding, not the third.

## Which document wins

Two live documents used to give opposite orders and nothing ranked them. **This one wins, and
the worker contract with it.** A project's own `CLAUDE.md` — a template's, or an instance's —
describes its tree; it does not get to say who in this process may post outward, because the
half that may is a property of the process and not of the stack. Where a `CLAUDE.md` says *file
it immediately*, it is describing **the orchestrator's half**, which is true, and it is not
addressing a dispatched worker, which cannot.

And the label is **never** a thing a document writes down. `sdd-ownership` computes it from
GitHub's own record of the lineage — `from-template` from a template, `from-instance` from an
instance — so a `--label` written into an instruction is a value that was right once. Fourteen
issues in this register carry `from-template` and were raised from an instance repository; that
is what a typed label looks like a year later, and it is why no verb below takes one.

## What you do

Three steps, in this order. They cost one command and one paragraph.

1. **Bank it, then file it — and do not stop to ask.** Banking is first because it cannot fail:

   ```bash
   sdd-engine change_state add-fault --cr <CR> --signal '<what it did, and what it cost>' \
     --owner engine
   ```

   `--owner` is the judgement and it takes one of three words: `engine`, `template`, or `here`
   for a fault this level owns and repairs rather than files.
   It writes the fault into the change record with the destination and its label **computed**,
   allocates it a `PROC-n`, and refuses nothing for want of a network. A second report of the
   same fault inside one change is the same row with `seen` counted up, not a second ticket.
   Then `fault-report` fills the form and runs one `gh issue create` against the address that
   was computed, and:

   ```bash
   sdd-engine change_state resolve-fault --cr <CR> --id PROC-n --filed <url>
   ```

   Do not search for a duplicate first — a duplicate costs a close and a link, a report lost
   with the session that found it costs the evidence. This is the intake rule that already
   governs a template filing upward, and it governs this for the same reason.

   **`gh` absent, unauthenticated, issues disabled, no network?** That costs the filing and it
   does not cost the finding: `resolve-fault --id PROC-n --unfiled --reason '<which of those>'`
   is a legal ending, the retro reports it, and the work carries on.
2. **Record the workaround where somebody will find it.** § 12 of the form has the field, and
   it asks the question that matters: must this be reverted when the fix lands, and where does
   the revert belong. *A workaround nobody removes becomes the behaviour.*
3. **Go on with the work.** The ticket is the record, not a gate. Cite its URL in the pull
   request body and in the change record or the changelog entry.

## Who files, and who reports

**A dispatched worker never files.** It touches no git, asks no user and posts nothing outward
— rules 2, 7 and 11. What it does is say so in one line of its closing block:

```
- PROCESS_FAULT: NONE | <the signal, and what it cost>
```

The orchestrator reads every report and files from the main conversation, before the stage
closes. **It banks the line in the same write that banks the return**, which is the mechanism
rather than the rule:

```bash
sdd-engine loop back --member <skill> --process-fault <skill>='engine:<the line it reported>'
```

That flag exists because the line used to have one reader and one fate. It reached the
orchestrator's context and nowhere else, so a wave that ended before it was acted on ended the
finding with it — and there was no moment at which anybody could see that a fault had been
reported and never filed. Now the queue is in the record, `loop next` carries the open ones in
its digest every turn, and the only way one leaves is with a URL or with a reason.

`sdd-retro` is the backstop and not the mechanism: it *reads the queue*, records which faults
were filed and names the ones that were not, and it files nothing itself — a skill that finds
and files its own findings is a skill grading its own work. Before the queue it had nothing to
read, so it was discovering for the first time, hours later, that nothing had been filed.

## What this rule does not do

**It is not a licence to skip the step.** A filed ticket says the process was in your way; it
does not say you may go around it. Where a refused preflight, a red gate or a hook's refusal
stands between you and the work, it still stands after you have filed — *"a refused preflight
is not something you work around."*

**It is not for an ordinary failure.** A test that fails, a gate that is red, a requirement
that contradicts another: those have their own routes — the debug ladder, the coherence gate,
`NEEDS_DECISION`. This is for when the *process itself* was the obstacle.

**It is not a counter.** One issue per distinct fault. Filing the same thing four times in one
session is noise, and noise is how a signal stops being read: *a rule with a false alarm
produces a red people silence, and then it stops working where it was right as well.* The
queue takes the cheap half of that off you — two members of one wave reporting the same fault
land on one `PROC-n` with `seen: 2` — and leaves the judgement, which is yours.

**It is not a gate.** Nothing in `close_stage` reads the queue. A fault that could not be filed
because somebody's token expired must not stop the product work that has nothing to do with it;
the digest carries it, the retro reports it, and neither refuses. An unfiled fault is a visible
debt, never a blocked stage.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/skills/fault-report

# File the fault against the repository that owns it

```bash
sdd-engine change_state add-fault --cr <CR> --signal '<what it did, and what it cost>' \
  --owner engine
sdd-ownership
gh issue create --repo <owner/repo> --label <label> \
  --title "[<stack>] <what must become true>" --body-file <body-path>
sdd-engine change_state resolve-fault --cr <CR> --id PROC-n --filed <url>
```

`--owner` takes one of three words — `engine`, `template`, or `here` for a fault this level
owns and repairs rather than files. It is the § 8 judgement, and the only thing in these four
lines you supply rather than compute.

**Bank it first.** `add-fault` writes the fault into the change record with its destination and
label already computed, and it cannot fail for want of a network — so the evidence, which is
your session's and expires with it, survives a `gh` that is missing, unauthenticated or
refused. Nothing after this line can lose it. Where there is no change record to bank into —
a fault found outside a change — go straight to `sdd-ownership` and say in your report that
there was no queue to use.

`sdd-ownership` prints the level and both addresses. **Run it and use what it printed** — the
destination is the one thing a session must not supply from memory, because a ticket filed in
the wrong repository is worse than none: it is evidence, in a place nobody who can act on it
will look. The same goes for `--label`: it is `from-template` from a template and
`from-instance` from an instance, it is computed from GitHub's own record of the lineage, and
a label typed from memory is how fourteen issues raised from an instance came to carry the
template's.

The rule this skill serves, and when it fires:
[`/Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/skills/_shared/process-failure.md`](../_shared/process-failure.md).

## Before anything: which level is this, and is there anything to file?

| `sdd-ownership` says | What you do |
|---|---|
| `flow` | **Stop, and say so.** You are in the marketplace checkout: the engine is underfoot and the fault is fixable here, through the ordinary change flow in `CLAUDE.md`. There is no upstream to file to, and an issue against the repository you are standing in is a note to yourself with extra steps. |
| `template` | The engine's fault goes up. A fault this template owns is fixed here, in this repository, not filed. |
| `instance` | Both go up, to different places. Decide which in § 8 of the form before you pick a destination. |
| `unknown` (exit 4) | **Stop and quote the gap it printed.** It names what could not be determined — `gh` absent, no remote, or a repository GitHub knows as neither a template nor made from one. Ask the user which repository owns this, once, and do not guess: the three destinations are three different teams' inboxes. |

## Whose fault is it? That is the judgement, and it is the one you must make

`sdd-ownership` settles the **address**. It does not settle the **owner**, and nothing can:
that is a reading of the evidence.

| The fault is | Where it goes |
|---|---|
| the engine contradicts its own documentation, or a skill instructs something impossible on this stack | the engine |
| the engine does what its documentation says, and the documentation is wrong or silent | the engine — and say so plainly in § 4: the ticket is a design question, and the fix may be a document |
| the template's scripts, its specification seed, its `.specconf/`, its CI or its own `CLAUDE.md` | the template, from an instance; fixed here, from the template itself |
| this repository's own application or specification | **neither.** Fix it here. A level asking the one above it to absorb its own bug is the failure § 8 of the form exists to catch |

When you cannot place it, file it at the engine with § 7 marked `HYPOTHESIS` and § 8 saying
you could not. An honest "I could not tell" routes faster than a confident wrong answer — the
triager reads § 8 first and reassigns.

## Fill the form, then file it

1. **Copy the form.** `forms/engine.md` for a fault the engine owns, `forms/template.md` for
   one a template owns. They are skeletons: the authority for what each section holds is the
   destination's own `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/forge-change-request.md`, and `forms/engine.md`
   mirrors its section list, held there by a test.
2. **Write the filled body to a file OUTSIDE the repository.** Not under `.sdd/` — the
   `PreToolUse` guard refuses every write there and is right to, and not inside the change
   directory either, where it would be committed as an artefact of the change. A temporary
   directory is fine.
3. **Paste the evidence, do not paraphrase it.** § 3 takes the command, its output and its
   exit code verbatim. A paraphrased error message has already lost the detail that identifies
   it, and your session is the last one that will have it.
4. **Check the label exists before you use it.** `gh issue create` refuses an unknown label
   and refuses the whole issue with it — after you have written the body.

   ```bash
   gh label list --repo <owner/repo> --search <label>
   ```

   If it is not there, **file without `--label` and say so in your report**. Creating a label
   in somebody else's repository is not this skill's business, and a report that landed
   unlabelled is a report that landed.
5. **File it, once.** Print the URL the command returns.
6. **Close the queue entry.** `resolve-fault --id PROC-n --filed <url>` if it landed, and
   `--unfiled --reason '<which of them>'` if it did not — `gh` absent, unauthenticated, issues
   disabled, the label refused and the whole issue with it. Both are endings the record keeps;
   the one thing it will not keep is a fault that was banked and never answered, which is what
   `sdd-retro` reads out at the end.

## Do not stop to ask, and do not look for a duplicate first

This is the opposite of skill `task-add`'s rule, and the difference is deliberate rather than
an inconsistency. A board item is the **user's** work item and posting one is a decision about
their board, so `task-add` asks. This is **evidence**, and it expires with the session that
holds it: the command, the exit code, the state of the tree. A duplicate costs a close and a
link; a report lost with its window costs the thing nobody can reconstruct.

So: file at the moment you find it, without a round trip through the user, and without
searching the issue list first. De-duplication is the triager's job and they have the whole
list in front of them; you have one session.

**One issue per distinct fault.** Filing the same thing four times in one session is noise,
and noise is how a signal stops being read.

## Then go on

The ticket is the record, not a gate. After filing:

- **Record the workaround** where somebody will find it — § 12 of the form asks where it is and
  whether it must be reverted. *A workaround nobody removes becomes the behaviour.*
- **Cite the URL** in the pull request body and in the change record or the changelog entry.
- **Carry on with the work.** A filed ticket says the process was in your way; it does not say
  you may go around it. A refused preflight, a red gate and a hook's refusal all still stand
  after you have filed.

## A worker never calls this skill

A dispatched worker touches no git, asks no user and posts nothing outward — rules 2, 7 and 11
of the worker contract. It reports the fault in one line of `PROCESS_FAULT` in its closing
block; the orchestrator banks that line with `loop back --process-fault` and files from the
main conversation, before the stage closes. This skill is for the half of the session that can
file. A project's `CLAUDE.md` that orders an immediate filing is addressing this half, and the
precedence is settled in one place:
[`process-failure.md` § Which document wins](../_shared/process-failure.md).

`sdd-retro` is the backstop and not the mechanism: it reads the queue, and its `audit.md`
records which faults were filed and names the ones that were not. It files nothing itself — a
skill that finds and files its own findings is a skill grading its own work.

## When it will not work

| Condition | What it is, and the fix |
|---|---|
| `gh` is not installed or not authenticated | Nothing here is a workaround. The fault is already banked — `add-fault` needs no network — so end it with `resolve-fault --unfiled --reason`, tell the user to run `gh auth login`, and carry on. The retro reads the queue and names it. |
| `sdd-ownership` exits 4 | The level is undetermined and it printed why. Ask the user which repository owns this. Never fall back to "the engine" because it is the one you know. |
| `gh issue create` refuses the label | The destination does not carry it. File without it and say so. |

sdd-engine change_state ask-question --cr <CR> --from-json <file.json>

[
  {
    "question": "Can a task exist with nobody assigned to it?",
    "allow_free_text": true,
    "blocks": ["COH-design-3"],
    "blocking": false,
    "options": [
      {"key": "A", "label": "Yes, nobody assigned means 'up for grabs'",
       "recommended": true,  "consequence": "A task can be opened before anyone knows who will do it"},
      {"key": "B", "label": "No, a person is required",
       "recommended": false, "consequence": "Nobody will record a task 'for later'"}
    ]
  }
]

Exactly one option has `recommended: true` and stands first -- a panel with no recommendation
pushes onto the user the analysis that was the process's job.

`qid` is optional and normally left out: the record allocates the next free `Q-n` per item,
in array order, and prints them back as `qids`. You could not compute it in any case, since
the ids in use are in `change.json` and `action_log.jsonl` and both are out of bounds here.
Asking the same question again while it is still open returns the id it already has.

`blocks` names what waits for the answer -- coherence findings, repair tasks, the members
this decides. Leave it out and the question holds the whole stage, which is what a question
with no `blocks` has always done. Name ids and it holds those and nothing else: the rest of
the pass moves while the person thinks. It can never hold nothing -- the stage's gate still
refuses to close over a question raised in it that is still open.

`blocking` is about WHEN it is asked, not what it holds: true sends it out at once instead
of waiting for the wave in the air to land. Justify it in the question's own text.
The contract for both: skills/_shared/question-policy.md.

- **severity:** minor
- **decision_mode:** HITL
- **auto_basis:**
- **ambiguity_source:** spec/invariants.md § Data invariants
- **artifacts:** CLAUDE.md, spec/README.md, contracts/invariants/todo_list.md

reconcile-docs in this stage:
- :128-131: "Deleting it deletes with it: … the contracts `contracts/openapi/guestbook.yaml` and
  `contracts/invariants/guestbook.md`".
- :136: "**One thing moves before the guestbook goes: the words of the text rule.**"

`spec/README.md`:63-65 carries the same deletion list. ADR-0001 § Consequences (:107-110) names the
same single move.

`contracts/invariants/todo_list.md` was written by the convergence round in this stage:
- :9-10: "`D-01`…`D-04` stand in `guestbook.md`, and the first three hold for `todo_tasks` as for
  every table".
- `D-05`, at :19-20: "It is `D-04` for the to-do list's one field".

Three more citations survive the deletion:
- `spec/design/data-model.md` § Identifiers (:72-74) points `D-03` into `guestbook.md`;
- § `todo_tasks` (:199) says "the counterpart of `D-04`";
- `spec/design/testing.md`:803 says the same.

**Why they cannot both be true.** Suppose someone follows the list and moves only `BR-01`'s words.
The context that stays then loses the three invariants its table is held to. Command: `python3`,
running the witness reader's own heading pattern over `contracts/invariants/*.md` with
`guestbook.md` left out. Output: `without guestbook.md, defined: ['D-05'] | D-01..D-03 present:
False`. The same run lists `D-04` still cited at `contracts/invariants/todo_list.md`:9 and :19,
`spec/design/data-model.md`:199, and `spec/design/testing.md`:547, :738, :803 and :1009.

Three checks would then go red:
- `tests/fitness/test_invariant_witnesses.py`:115 asserts `{"D-01", "D-02", "D-03"} <= found`.
- `frozen-ids` goes red on every citation of `D-04`, because it holds the `D-xx` space
  (`spec/glossary.md` § Identifiers and their spaces: "an identifier named in prose and defined
  nowhere goes red").
- `links` goes red on `contracts/invariants/todo_list.md`:10.

So "one thing moves" is false. `D-01`…`D-04` would have to move too, with their identifiers, because
`contracts/invariants/README.md` § Identifiers says they are "never renamed, never reused", and a
superseded one keeps its heading.

content.content:
text the rules refuse, aimed at a task somebody has deleted.
  **Now:** `BR-13` states that such a correction is told the text's reason, on the screen and by
  the application alike, because the screen refuses the text before anything is sent. Only a
  change that could otherwise be made learns that its task no longer exists.
  **Why:** As written, the bold sentence of `BR-13` was false for one case the build handles on purpose. The service judges a correction's text before it writes, and the lookup is the write itself, so a refused text is refused for its text whatever task it names (`judge_todo_task_text` runs before the one `UPDATE` in `change_todo_task`). The contract publishes that order as "the lookup last" (`spec/design/api.md` § The to-do list's refusals), and `test_a_request_is_refused_for_what_it_is_whatever_its_identifier_names` holds it under `CR-2609-823a/R-8`. The screen cannot behave any other way: `BR-06` forbids it to let through a text the application would refuse, so the editor refuses that text before sending anything, and a person there never learns that the task is gone. `R-6` clause 4 and `R-8` clause 1 both apply to this case and name different reasons. ### The design phase -- what the change wrote into the specification

-- `MODIFIED` `spec/design/api.md` — the opening sentence; § Routes and their contexts (two rows); § Shapes (`TodoTaskRead`, `TodoTaskList`, `TodoTaskCreate`, `TodoTaskUpdate`, added after the guestbook's four); § Endpoints (four rows, and the subsection "The to-do list's endpoints"); § Refusals (the subsection "The to-do list's refusals", after the guestbook's body example). Every other paragraph is byte-identical.

-  **Was:** the register described one context: its opening named `spec/contexts/guestbook.md` as where the rules are, the route table had three rows, and every shape, endpoint and refusal code was the guestbook's or the health probe's.

-  **Now:** the opening names both context documents; `/api/todo-tasks` (`GET`, `POST`) and `/api/todo-tasks/{todo_task_id}` (`PATCH`, `DELETE`) are registered to `todo_list`; four shapes are stated field by field, with read and write kept apart; four endpoints with their cardinality; and five stable refusal codes — `todo_task_not_found` (404), `todo_task_empty_patch`, `todo_task_text_empty`, `todo_task_text_multiline`, `todo_task_text_too_long` (422) — each with its finished sentence, whether it carries `id`, and the one order in which a request earns exactly one of them.

-  **Why:** Two implementers build this boundary at the same time without talking, so every question they could answer differently is answered here once: that marking and correcting are one `PATCH` whose absent fields are never written, which is what lets a correction and a marking sent at the same moment both stick (`BR-10`, race `W-1`) and makes a marking set the chosen state instead of flipping the stored one (`BR-09`, race `W-2`); that a missing task answers `404` and is never created again (`BR-13`, race `W-3`); that the list is one envelope holding every task in one total order with no parameters (`BR-11`); and that a task's text is refused with one of three codes a caller can branch on, in the order `BR-07` fixes, because the requirements demand a reason of its own for a line break (`R-2` clause 6, `Q-11`) and the scenarios tell "no text", "too long" and "more than one line" apart (`S-6`, `S-8`, `S-33`), which the integration corpus test proves on the wire and which FastAPI's list of Pydantic errors cannot do in words this contract owns. The standing rule of § Refusals — a stable code, a finished sentence, a status code with two shapes published as two — is applied to the new resource rather than restated.

# SDD Retro

<prerequisites>
## PREREQUISITES

### Stage 1 — Automated checks

    sdd-skill sdd-retro scripts/retro_capture.py preflight

**Read what it prints. Do not pipe it, do not truncate it, do not write a filter for it.**
It prints finished text now, precisely so there is nothing to parse — the JSON envelope it
used to print was run through `head -60` and through two hand-written `python3 -c` filters in
session `0d433f45`, which is how the size ratchet `MAX_ENVELOPE_BYTES` came to exist.

This is the only command called a preflight. `preflight.py` beside this file is the shared
conversational brief every skill has; the line above is the one that matters here, because it
seeds the summary and reports the size.

### Stage 2 — Preparation

None. **Do not open the transcript files** — they are megabytes of JSONL, you already lived
the session they record, and pulling them into context is the one action that can make this
skill cost more than everything it archives.

**Nothing in the pipeline depends on this skill, and nothing should** -- but since
2026-09-21 an ending no longer depends on it either. The `SessionEnd` hook archives the
bytes of every session, so the question this skill answers has narrowed to the one only
this session can answer: what it *meant*. The archive is no longer at risk if you are
interrupted; the meaning still is.

**And do not go looking for numbers either.** This skill produces no measurements at all.
Tokens, tool mix, rule breaches and the rest are computed once, for *every* session of this
repository, when the corpus is collected (`sdd-retro dump`) — where they cost no
context and cover far more than this one run. What only you have is the meaning.
</prerequisites>

<iron_rules>
## IRON RULES

1. **The archive is the product.** This skill captures raw material for an analysis somebody
   else performs later, across many sessions. Evidence you improved is evidence you destroyed.
2. **Never open a `.jsonl`, and never call a history tool.** Not the file, not
   `session_audit.py`, not `mcp__sdd-history__*`, not `mcp__claude-history__*`. The script
   copies the transcript; you never read it back. A summary written by re-reading the
   transcript is a summary of what you can still fit in context, which is the last third of
   the session — and an audit assembled from counters is an audit of what a counter can see.
   **Both documents come from the conversation you are in.** That is the only place holding
   why you chose this route, what you looked for and did not find, and where you turned back;
   none of it is in the record, and no tool can recover it once this context is gone.
3. **Never dispatch a subagent.** Two reasons, and either alone is enough: a subagent writes
   into `subagents/` inside the very tree being copied, so the capture would race its own
   evidence; and a fresh context has no session to audit, so the judgement it returned would
   be about nothing.
4. **`summary.md` proposes nothing. `audit.md` judges.** The witness records what happened
   and never what should have happened instead; the judge says plainly what went wrong. Two
   files because the rules are opposite: one must stay an unimproved sample, the other must
   be blunt. Never let either leak into the other.
5. **A claim is not evidence, including your own.** "The tests pass" is a claim; the exit code
   of `./scripts/check.sh` is evidence. Where you cannot produce evidence, write the claim
   down as unverified rather than softening it into probably true.
6. **Look for the bent rule, not the broken one.** A rule broken outright fails a gate. A rule
   *bent* — a requirement written vaguer so it was easier to satisfy, a test asserting less
   than the requirement it cites, a delta `**Why:**` that restates the change — passes
   everything, and is the whole reason this half of the skill exists.
7. **A root cause is a hypothesis until you have read the code.** When a finding blames a
   deterministic failure — a `fail()` in a script, a validator, a preflight, a gate — and you
   have not read that code in this session, write "probably, to be confirmed in
   `file.py`" and name the file. A confidently wrong cause routes the repair at the wrong
   thing while looking exactly like a repair.
8. **Fix nothing, and file nothing.** Not the code, not the skills, not the rules, and not an
   issue against any of them. Repair is a separate round, run from
   `/Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/retro-prompts/`. A skill that finds and fixes is a skill grading its own work,
   and one that finds and files is the same skill with a URL. What you DO owe a process
   finding is the question of whether anybody else will ever see it: for each bent rule, say
   whether it was filed and where, or that it was not. You are the backstop for
   `/Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/skills/_shared/process-failure.md`, not its mechanism — the session files, and you
   record what the session did.
9. **Commit with the verb, never by hand.** `commit` stages the archive and refuses anything
   else. `CR-2608-9373` carries a committed *unfilled* summary with no transcript and no
   manifest, swept in by `git add spec/changes/<CR>/` — five prose steps failed once already.
10. **Push, and let the project say whether to ask.** The session ends on the remote,
    because an archive on one laptop is one disk failure from gone and every reader of the
    corpus reads what was pushed. Whether a question precedes it is `boundary.push` in
    `.specconf/process.json`: `ask` puts it to the user with the megabytes and the
    personal-data counts above it; `auto` pushes and then says what it did. Read the
    setting, never guess it — `plan-push` prints it. Decision of 2026-08-22 made this a
    push at all; the setting was added when the retro became a beat of every stage
    boundary, because a question asked eight times per change is a question nobody reads.
11. **An empty section is data.** A section with nothing in it says "this did not happen". A
    section you fill by inventing contaminates the count it feeds.
</iron_rules>

<role>
## ROLE

You are the **archivist and the cold reviewer** of the session you are in — in that order,
and the order matters: archive first, judge second, because the judgement must not be able to
edit the evidence it is about.

**Expertise:**
- Writing a summary that is still legible as the fortieth row of a table
- Telling what happened from what you concluded about what happened
- Knowing which facts are already measured and which only you can supply

**Mindset:**
- **The transcript records what was done; you record why it changed.** A person changing their
  mind mid-sentence leaves no marker anywhere in the JSONL. That is your section.
- **You are the one reader who cannot judge whether the documents were clear**, because you
  were here. Ask what a person who was not here would have made of them.
- **Praise is cheap and useless.** So is a manufactured problem. Be genuinely critical, and do
  not invent a finding to look thorough.
- **Stable headings beat good prose.** Both documents will be read by a script before they are
  read by a person.

<context>
## PURPOSE & CONTEXT

**Context.** The SDD process is judged from its own traces, and for a long time nothing kept
them: transcripts expire quietly under `~/.claude/projects/` on Claude Code's own schedule.
Two skills used to split this job — one archived and was forbidden to think, one thought and
was never once invoked in 76 sessions, leaving no artefact anywhere. Half of its rubric
restated the summary's own sections. They are one skill now.

**Goal.** One directory per session inside the change record: the raw transcript, a structured
summary, an audit written from the conversation, and an empty `feedback.md` waiting for
the user — committed, so a question asked in six months has three independent sentences about
the same run behind it. Three, because that is the smallest number that shows what the agent
does not know about itself: the summary says what happened, the audit says how the agent
judges it, and the feedback says how the person who sat through it judges it.

**What this skill catches:**
- A session whose only record was a context that got cleared
- A decision taken in conversation and written down nowhere else
- The instruction sentence somebody hesitated at, which no script can reconstruct
- A claim this session made that its own state does not support
- A rule bent rather than broken, which every gate passed

<common_rationalizations>
## COMMON RATIONALIZATIONS

| Excuse | Reality |
|---|---|
| "I will skim the transcript to write a better summary" | It is megabytes of JSONL and you lived the session. Skimming gets you the last third and costs more than the archive is worth. |
| "The summary looks thin, I will add some analysis" | Analysis has its own file. A thin summary of a thin session is a correct summary. |
| "Section 6 is empty, I will find something" | Then the session had no friction, and that is a data point. Inventing one poisons the count it feeds. |
| "I will quote the guilty sentence and say what it should say" | The quote is section 7 of the summary; what it should say is a finding in `audit.md`. Both exist — put each where it belongs. |
| "The audit found nothing, so there is nothing to write" | Write what you checked. An unstated clean check reads as a check nobody ran. |
| "I ran the tests earlier, they passed" | Earlier is not now and there have been edits. Run them, or record the claim as unverified. |
| "The subagent said it wrote the file" | Then the file exists and `git status` shows it. If you did not look, that is exactly the finding. |
| "This rule was bent for a good reason" | Then the reason is a finding, and it belongs where somebody can agree with it. |
| "I know why that script refused" | Do you, in this session? If you did not read it, mark the cause a hypothesis and name the file. |
| "I will fix this small thing while I am here" | Then the audit cannot be checked and the fix arrives unreviewed. Report it. |
| "`git add spec/changes/<CR>/` is simpler" | It is how a half-written archive got committed once already. Use `commit`. |
| "Capture warned about size, I will pass `--force`" | `--force` is for a source that shrank, not for a repository that grew. Say the number to the user. |
| "There is no change record but this session mattered" | Hard stop. Archive into the change this work belonged to, from its branch. |

<workflow>
## WORKFLOW

### Phase 1: Preflight

- [ ] `sdd-skill sdd-retro scripts/retro_capture.py preflight`
- [ ] A refusal — say what it printed and stop
- [ ] Over 20 MB — say the number to the user before going on

### Phase 2: Capture

- [ ] `sdd-skill sdd-retro scripts/retro_capture.py capture`
- [ ] Read the personal-data counts and the path list it printed
- [ ] Copy nothing by hand. If the script did not copy it, it is not in the archive
- [ ] This is a first copy, not the last one: `commit` re-copies the transcript, so the
      turns this phase and the next three take land in the archive too. That tail used to
      be lost -- 21.5 % of the corpus of CR-2608-8e96, and the part where the
      orchestrator improvises hardest
- [ ] **An archive may already be there, and finding one is not a sign anything went
      wrong.** The `SessionEnd` hook writes a minimal one at every ending, marked
      `partial` -- bytes only, no summary and no audit, because a session nobody remembers
      must not be given a narrative. Your `capture` takes it out of `partial` and section
      10 of the summary is rewritten, not appended to. Nothing is deleted and nothing has
      to be cleaned up first

### Phase 3: Audit

- [ ] `sdd-skill sdd-retro scripts/retro_capture.py audit`
- [ ] Read the numbers and the user's notes from today. The script writes the mechanical half
      of `sessions/<session-id>/audit.md`; you append the judgement
- [ ] For each load-bearing claim this session made — the gate is green, the tests cover the
      requirements, the specification records what was built, the file list is complete — name
      the command that would falsify it and **run it**. Five steps:
      `/Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/skills/_shared/verification.md`
- [ ] Look for the bent rules: a requirement vaguer than the conversation; a test asserting
      less than the requirement it cites; a delta `**Why:**` restating the change; a stage
      advanced on a report rather than a refreshed preflight; an ambiguity resolved by
      inference instead of a question; scope in the diff nobody agreed to
- [ ] For each bent rule that is a fault in the PROCESS rather than in this change — a step
      improvised because none was written, a script run to get past something, a hatch spent,
      an instruction naming a file that is not there — write **whether it was filed, and
      where**: the issue URL, or that it was not and why not. **`audit` printed the queue**
      (`THIS CHANGE'S PROCESS FAULTS`), so this is read off a list rather than out of memory:
      each `PROC-n` with its state, its computed destination, and the URL or the reason. A
      fault that reached no repository is the finding this sentence exists to surface — and a
      queue with nothing in it is itself a claim to check, because a session that worked
      around the process and reported nothing leaves exactly that. You do not file it now; you
      record that it is unfiled, and the user decides in **For the user to decide**
- [ ] Fill the seven sections of `audit.md` **from this conversation**:
      **Verified** (claim, command, result), **Unverified**, **Divergences**,
      **Bent rules**, **Checked and clean**, **What worked**,
      **For the user to decide**. The list is `retro_capture.AUDIT_SECTIONS` — one list,
      because this checklist and the template both read it. Every finding carries
      evidence; every deterministic cause you did not read is marked a hypothesis with
      its file named
- [ ] **What worked** is not padding and not praise. A round that reads only defects
      learns only what to avoid, and a process also has to know what to keep. Name what
      held, with the same evidence discipline as a defect
- [ ] Remove the `<!-- SESSION DRAFT: … -->` line when the audit is filled. `verify` refuses
      while it stands — a template committed as an audit reads exactly like a session that
      noticed nothing wrong
- [ ] Tell the user where `feedback.md` is. It is the third sentence about this run: the
      summary says what happened, the audit says how you judge it, and both are yours.
      Empty is fine and `verify` accepts it — but it is the one thing in this archive no
      number can replace

### Phase 4: Write the summary

Fill `sessions/<session-id>/summary.md` in place, from the conversation you are in — never by
reading the transcript back. Front matter first, then all ten headings.

- [ ] Sections 1–3 — what was asked, what happened, what was produced
- [ ] Sections 4–5 — decisions and questions, the two things the transcript cannot show as such
- [ ] Sections 6–8 — friction, hesitations, workarounds. **Quote; do not prescribe** — the
      prescription belongs in `audit.md`
- [ ] Section 9 — what was not done
- [ ] Remove the `<!-- SESSION DRAFT:` marker. While it is there the file counts as unfilled,
      and `verify` will refuse

### Phase 5: Verify and commit

- [ ] `sdd-skill sdd-retro scripts/retro_capture.py verify`
- [ ] Non-zero — fix what it names and run it again
- [ ] `sdd-skill sdd-retro scripts/retro_capture.py commit`
- [ ] It re-copies the transcript, records the artefact, stages the session directory plus
      the record that names it, and commits. **Do not assemble these steps by hand**
- [ ] Called twice on a session that has not moved, the second is `empty` and grows no
      history. A second commit means the session grew, and that is worth having
- [ ] Say the megabytes and the personal-data counts out loud, and that
      `git reset --soft HEAD~1` undoes the commit

### Phase 6: Ask, then push

An archive that lives on one laptop is an archive one disk failure away from gone, and
every reader of the corpus — `sdd_history`'s `repo` source, the round package, a fresh
clone — reads what was pushed. So the session ends by pushing. Whether it asks first is the
project's setting, not your reading of the moment.

- [ ] `sdd-engine checkpoint plan-push` — it prints the branch,
      the base, the commit count and **which mode this project is in**
- [ ] `boundary.push: "auto"` → push it and then report: `python3
      /Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/skills/_shared/sdd/checkpoint.py push --at-boundary`. Say the megabytes and
      the personal-data counts from Phase 5 **after** it, in the same message. The setting
      is the authorisation; asking anyway makes it meaningless
- [ ] `boundary.push: "ask"` → ask with the printed payload, **recommending yes**, with the
      megabytes and the personal-data counts above the question. The user decided on
      2026-08-22 that a retro ends with a push; the question is one click, not a debate,
      and it exists because the thing being pushed is raw transcripts
- [ ] On a yes: `sdd-engine checkpoint push --confirmed`
- [ ] On a no: say the commit stands locally and name the same command for later
- [ ] `--at-boundary` is refused in `ask` mode and `--confirmed` is refused without a
      question. Neither flag is the other one spelled differently: one says a person was
      asked just now, the other that a person configured this once
</workflow>

<error_handling>
## ERROR HANDLING

| Condition | Action |
|---|---|
| No change record on this branch | Hard stop. This skill runs on the change branch before the merge. Switch to it, or open a change with `sdd-engine cr new "<title>" --request "<verbatim>"`. |
| No transcript for this session | Exit 2. The record has been pruned. `session_analysis.py` looks in every project directory this repository owns, including worktrees, so this really means gone — nothing here can be reconstructed from memory. |
| No session id in the environment | Hard stop. `/Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/skills/_shared/sdd/session_id.py` names the variable it wanted. |
| `total_bytes` unusually large | Say the megabytes to the user and ask before capturing. A repository grows in one direction only. |
| Personal-data shapes non-zero | Report the counts. Raw capture is the deliberate decision, but the commit must not be the first time anybody sees the number. |
| Capture reports a smaller archive than before | The source was rotated or truncated. Say so; `--force` records the fact, it does not repair anything. |
| `verify` says a sha256 moved | The session wrote more while you were summarising. Run `capture` again, then `verify`. |
| `verify` says `audit.md` is missing | Run `audit`, then append the six sections. An archive with no judgement leaves the next reader counting rows and guessing why. |
| `commit` refuses: something else is staged | Unstage it. This commit carries the archive and nothing else; that rule exists because it was broken once. |
| `.git/index.lock` present | Another git operation is in flight. Wait and retry; this is contention, not failure. |
| The change is not yet at `deliver` | Commit anyway — the archive belongs on the branch. Warn that gate `change-record` will hold the pull request until the change itself is ready. |
| A finding needs a rule change | Record it in **For the user to decide** and stop. Repair is a separate round, from `/Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/retro-prompts/`. |
| The summary would repeat what `audit` already counted | Leave it to the numbers. Sections 4 to 8 are the ones only you can write. |
</error_handling>

<quality_gate>
## QUALITY GATE

Verification before every declaration of completion: [`/Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/skills/_shared/verification.md`](../_shared/verification.md) — five steps, the claim→evidence table, and `UNVERIFIED` when the evidence cannot be obtained on this machine.

### Stage 1 — Automated checks

    sdd-skill sdd-retro scripts/retro_capture.py verify

### Stage 2 — Review before returning

1. **`verify` exited 0.** STOP if: it did not.
2. **All ten summary headings are present**, and the `<!-- SESSION DRAFT:` marker is gone. STOP
   if: a heading was dropped because its section was empty.
3. **No proposal anywhere in `summary.md`.** Search it for "I propose", "we should",
   "worth adding". STOP if: any appears — that sentence belongs in `audit.md`.
4. **Every finding in `audit.md` names its evidence**, and every deterministic root cause you
   did not read in this session is marked a hypothesis with its file named. STOP if: a cause
   is asserted as fact on a file you never opened.
5. **`audit.md` lists what was checked and found clean.** STOP if: it reports only problems —
   a reader cannot tell that from an audit that looked at three things.
6. **Nothing was fixed.** Run `git status --porcelain`; the only paths touched are under
   `sessions/<session-id>/`. STOP if: anything else changed.
7. **The push was asked, not assumed.** STOP if: `git log origin/<branch>..HEAD` is empty
   and no `AskUserQuestion` about the push is in this session — that is a push nobody
   authorised, and this is the one step that leaves the machine.
8. **The size and the shape counts were said to the user.** STOP if: the report omits them.
</quality_gate>

<bottom_line>
## BOTTOM LINE

**Run the preflight, let the script copy the transcript, then run `audit` and read the numbers
it gives you — never the transcript itself, which is megabytes of JSONL recording a session
you already lived. Write two documents, because they answer to opposite rules: `summary.md`
is the witness and proposes nothing, so that whoever counts across forty sessions gets a
sample nobody improved; `audit.md` is the judge and says plainly what went wrong, with a
command behind every claim and the word "probably" in front of every cause whose code
you did not read. Leave empty the sections that were empty, because an empty section says
"this did not happen" and an invented one poisons the count it feeds. Fix nothing — repair is
a separate round from `/Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/retro-prompts/`. Commit with `commit`, never by hand, because the five
steps it replaces already failed once and left a committed empty template behind. Say the
megabytes and the personal-data counts out loud, and then ask to push and push: an archive
that never leaves the laptop is an archive the next round cannot read.**
</bottom_line>
